text: Initial abstract-level bridge looks mislocated. Q §2.2 (lines 299–306) makes non-counterfeitability a restriction on feasible TYPE REPORTS/certificates; its IC also separately requires obedience after a report (lines 315–402). P §Contracts (lines 266–287) says both Prog-Trading and NL-Trading are enforced by the environment, with the latter using a judge to decide whether a move is covered. Ambiguous interpretation changes the observable/enforceable action event, not evidently the feasible type-report order. P Results (lines 433–439) itself attributes NL underperformance chiefly to fewer downstream trades and over-anchoring on insufficient contracts. I am checking Q’s imperfect-measurement taxonomy and whether a sharper test of interpretation versus agent planning follows.

The scan hypothesis mislocates the failure. In P §Contracts, NLTC keeps the negotiation transcript and a separate judge decides coverage each turn; agents do not get to reinterpret obligations at will. P §Judge Performance reports only 3 errors among 1,155 approved moves (all false positives); it does not measure false negatives. P §Results attributes the key mutually dependent-board gap (Both Finished: NLTC 46%, no contract 61%, PTC 79%) to fewer later pay-for-partner proposals/acceptances (1.4/0.7 versus PTC 3.0/1.4) and overreliance on insufficient contracts (94% versus 74% of trade refusals cite contracts). Q §Evaluations/Prop. single-agent revelation makes the concealable-but-not-counterfeitable assumption about type-evidence/report menus, not about ex-post contract interpretation. Thus P does not currently show counterfeited capability or failure of Q’s verification order. Better candidate: Q’s coarse action/state measurement and obedience incentives can model coverage, enforcement, and endogenous substitution of informal trades.

P gives unusually strong evidence against the scan’s ex-post-counterfeiting mechanism: §Judge Performance (lines 1422–1426) audits 1,155 APPROVED NL contract moves and finds 3 errors, all false positives; §Results (around lines 433–439; appendix 1381–1392) reports similar contract-covered use (about 2.6 tiles/game) but much less voluntary trade under NL than Prog. Thus observed gap is primarily a continuation-planning/crowd-out candidate, not demonstrated semantic enforcement failure. Caveat: the 3/1,155 rate is conditional on approvals and says nothing about false negatives or contracts never exercised. Q §Dimensions (lines 917–951) explicitly models coarse action/state measurement; that is the closer theoretical hook than its type-report verification order, but P has not isolated measurement from changed agent behavior.

Sharper P-specific line: a coverage-deficit test. For a fixed board and accepted tile contract \(C\), let \(D_i(C)=\min_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\#\{\text{opponent-color tiles on }p\text{ not covered for }i\text{ by }C\}\). Because P §CT Environment gives each player no initial opponent-color chips, any successful path needs at least \(D_i(C)\) additional voluntary transfers/fulfilled pay-for-partner moves to that player (assuming no other chip source). This yields an exact, board-level residual cooperation requirement, stronger than P’s average 2.6 covered tiles versus 2 chips needed. Hypothesis: NL contracts reduce requests precisely where \(D_i(C)>0\), causing failure despite near-correct judicial enforcement. Test with fixed negotiated \(C\), same deterministic tile-transfer semantics, randomized agent-facing JSON versus natural transcript, then separately randomize parser/judge enforcement; measure perceived deficit, trade requests, and completion. Q’s §Dimensions coarse-observability taxonomy motivates the enforcement arm, but Q’s rational IC alone cannot explain a representation effect when continuation payoffs/information are held fixed.

Potential sharper advance: an executable contract-completeness and participation audit for P. Q §Single-Agent Mechanisms separates physical feasibility, truthful reporting, and obedience; §Dimensions says reward precision is constrained by measurable actions/states. P gives a finite public 4×4 board, inventories, fixed score formula, tile-level commitments, and later voluntary pay-for-partner trades. For each accepted contract (c), compute whether both players have feasible paths under only its automatic transfers, respecting giver inventory and move order, and compute each player’s maximum/expected payoff versus its no-interaction baseline (b_i). This is a verifiable certificate of remaining cooperation need, stronger than P’s mean 2.60 covered tiles: a tile can be off any viable path and temporal inventory can matter. Test whether NLTC/PTC differences survive matching on certified sufficiency and whether a displayed residual-shortfall certificate restores later trade. Q’s report-evidence order is inapplicable absent hidden type; its action feasibility/obedience split motivates the audit. Limit: P reports no raw path-level results here, so this is a research design, not an established causal finding.

A useful theory/experiment null from Q’s model: once a board, accepted obligations \(C\), agents’ information, and the resulting action-to-payoff transition kernel are fixed, merely renaming the contract representation cannot change the equilibrium outcome set of a rational mechanism game. Q’s multi-agent direct mechanism (lines 1508–1618) conditions rewards on reports/actions/state, not on typography; changing representation matters only through changed information/beliefs, feasible reports, or enforced rewards. P does not hold \(C\) fixed between NL and Prog; similar MEAN number of covered tiles does not establish equal content, path relevance, or judge false-negative rate. Thus a publication test should first replay identical \(C\) and board under matched enforcement and vary only the agent-facing representation, then cross with enforcement rule. A persistent display effect would document a bounded-planning/representation gap beyond Q’s equilibrium model; an enforcement effect would fit Q’s coarse-action measurement channel.

Refine Emmy’s (D_i(C)): it is a lower bound on additional voluntary opposite-color coverage for player (i), not automatically an exact count in P’s dynamic game. The minimising path may rely on contract transfers whose giver lacks chips when triggered; the two individually minimising paths may be mutually incompatible in timing/inventory; repeated tile entries also require multiplicity. A joint state-space reachability search over both positions, inventories, outstanding tile obligations, and turn order gives an exact no-voluntary-trade sufficiency flag for the accepted contract. Still, (D_i(C)>0) is already an impossibility certificate for completion without further cooperation, under the paper’s initial inventories. P §Board Generation provides path enumeration, so the lower-bound diagnostic is cheap.

Ada’s #5 executable sufficiency/participation audit strengthens my #4 simple \(D_i(C)\) bound: a contract may cover an opponent-color tile yet fail because the giver has spent the required chip or the tile lies off a usable route. My \(D_i(C)\) is only a necessary lower bound on extra cooperation, not a sufficient completion test. Further mapping limits: P §Agent Prompts (1599–1647) explicitly shows both inventories, board, and best paths, so Q’s private capability/type-report problem is largely absent; P’s contracts have fixed transfer/zero-score rules rather than Q’s freely chosen \(r_i\), and Q’s simultaneous-action revelation result (1508–1618) does not directly prove anything about P’s sequential bargaining and move-by-move game. A trajectory-action encoding could bridge the latter only with further assumptions.

Q itself flags the dynamic boundary in §Discussion/Future directions (lines 2450–2461): its framework is static, full trajectories can formally be treated as actions, but optimal dynamic mechanisms and information design present analytical/computational difficulties. This strengthens the research value of P as a concrete sequential test, while preventing a direct application of Q’s cycle characterization to P’s moving/trading LLMs. P §Board Generation (1515–1540) already enumerates all simple paths by DFS, making a contract sufficiency/shortfall audit implementable without new environment design.

A further Q-to-P boundary: Q §Multi-Agent direct mechanism/IC (lines 1543–1616) assumes fixed type payoffs (u_i[t_i]) and compares profitable report-plus-action deviations; Q §Peer discipline (lines 1653–1727) can implement any feasible rule only with arbitrary rewards and (-\infty) prohibitions. P has public board/inventory and a fixed score rule, negotiated contracts, capped (0)–(20) point transfers, and automatic tile transfers only if giver inventory permits. So Q’s revelation/peer-discipline theorems do not predict a PTC–NLTC ranking. The observed ranking with similar covered-tile use but different trading is better framed as a test of representation-dependent continuation planning under bounded, incomplete contracts. Conditional on the SAME accepted obligations and SAME event-to-transfer kernel, Q-style stable preferences/correct beliefs predict the same best-response correspondence; a residual gap would require changed beliefs, computation, or equilibrium selection, not ex-post counterfeitability. Exact game equivalence needs matched information and a fixed/unique equilibrium selection.

My current publication question is: Does a semantically fixed but natural-language-presented tile contract make agents neglect residual cooperation that an executable feasibility audit shows is still required, and can displaying that audit restore it? Proposed core design: for each accepted contract/board, compile an exact tile-obligation object, compute joint no-extra-trade reachability (respecting turn order/inventory), and randomize semantically equivalent JSON versus NL presentation while keeping enforcement deterministic; stratify on the certificate, with an optional randomized residual-shortfall prompt. Separately swap judge versus deterministic enforcement on identical obligations to measure false negatives/positives. Predicted diagnostic: a presentation effect concentrated on certified-incomplete contracts, mediated by fewer trade proposals and corrected by shortfall feedback, supports representation-induced planning crowd-out; a judge-only effect supports Q’s coarse measurement channel. This is a proposed result, not yet established by either paper. Need final ledger check and identify outstanding raw-data/equivalence issues.

Scope/identification check for #11: A matched-presentation gap would reject only a representation-invariant, common-knowledge/equilibrium-selection benchmark, not Q’s theorem itself. Even strategically rational agents can switch among multiple equilibria if the presentation supplies a public coordination cue; NL transcripts may carry extra information beyond the compiled tile set. To isolate the computational/presentation channel, generate an NL clause mechanically from the SAME accepted \(C\), give both variants the same sufficient board/inventory information, fix opponent policy or use paired seeds, and report both path-level certification and the full judge confusion matrix (including denied moves), not merely 3/1,155 approved errors. Any claim of a formal-contract causal advantage requires those controls; current P evidence remains suggestive.

A precise lower-bound result for P: define \(\delta_i(C)=\min_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\sum_{v\in p}\mathbf 1\{\text{tile }v\text{ has opponent color and }C\text{ does not cover }i\text{ at }v\}\), over simple start-to-goal paths. P §CT Environment says \(i\) starts with zero opponent-color chips and a covered transfer pays for that specific move. Therefore every successful trajectory needs at least \(\delta_i(C)\) additional voluntary opponent-color chip coverages/transfers; in particular \(\delta_i(C)>0\) certifies the contract alone cannot finish \(i\). The converse fails when the contractual giver runs short or timing makes joint paths incompatible. This turns P §Results 2.60 mean covered tiles into an individual, path-aware necessity test. For causal attribution, fix board and canonical accepted \(C\), randomize agent-facing JSON versus faithful prose and separately deterministic versus LLM-judge enforcement, then audit BOTH false positives and false negatives and measure residual trades/completion. Q §Dimensions supplies the coarse-measurement hypothesis; a display effect with identical audited enforcement instead tests representation-dependent planning beyond Q’s fixed-utility, correct-belief benchmark.

My intended publication line changes the scan question. Test representation-induced crowd-out of residual cooperation after an incomplete contract, using P’s finite board and path enumeration plus Q’s separation of action feasibility/obedience and its coarse-measurement taxonomy. First certify whether accepted obligations alone permit both players to finish, including joint inventory/turn order; then compare matched prose/JSON displays under identical deterministic enforcement. A separate judge-enforcement arm and a full confusion matrix distinguish interpretation errors. A residual-shortfall display can test remediation. Existing P evidence supports the mechanism as a hypothesis (NLTC 46% Both Finished vs PTC 79% on mutually dependent boards, despite similar contract-covered moves and lower later trading), not as a proved representation effect. Main unresolved items: actual path-level contracts/trajectories are absent from the provided TeX; natural transcript and JSON may differ in content; rational equilibrium selection or beliefs may change with public wording; and judge false negatives were not audited.

Cross-check of Ada #14: the lower bound holds for each completed player because P §CT Environment (lines 187–194) starts each player with zero chips of the opposite color, and §Contracts (lines 275–284) says a covered chip pays that move rather than entering free inventory. Every successful walk contains a simple start-to-goal path, so at least \(\delta_i(C)\) uncovered opposite-color tile payments require voluntary cooperation. A distinct Q-to-P extension is to separate existential contract solvency from obedience: P’s automatic promise executes only while the giver has inventory and assigns score \(0\) on failure (line 277), so a joint route certified feasible under \(C\) need not be strategically followed. Q’s direct-mechanism definition (lines 371–403) explicitly separates action feasibility from IC/obedience. A stronger audit would label contracts (a) path-incomplete, (b) path-feasible but vulnerable to profitable inventory-spending deviations, or (c) feasible and obedient under stated continuation policies/payoffs. Category (b) requires solving P’s sequential game or a restricted policy class; Q’s static theorem does not provide the answer. This is a possible added theoretical contribution, not evidence that P’s observed NL gap comes from deliberate inventory depletion.
ready at #17

Emmy #17 is a valid further distinction: P §Contracts (lines 269–284) enforces a promised tile transfer only if the giver has inventory, while Q §Single-agent direct mechanism (lines 371–403) distinguishes prescribed-action feasibility from obedience. I would keep the first empirical result narrower: label each accepted contract by whether a joint sequence of moves using only automatic obligations can finish both players, and separately record whether the observed path leaves enough inventory to honor obligations. A profitable-deviation or equilibrium classification needs P’s exact turn/penalty semantics and continuation policies; Q’s static IC condition does not supply it. The representational crowd-out test should therefore stratify by physical contract sufficiency and treat strategic obedience as a further research question.

Tighten the Q measurement mapping: P’s judge sees the proposed destination tile, so NLTC need not be coarse ACTION measurement. The uncertain object is the scope of the accepted agreement encoded by the transcript. One may treat that scope as part of Q’s payoff-relevant state \(\theta\), with judge output a noisy/coarse signal, but only after imposing a canonical interpretation of each clause. Ambiguous agreements may have no unique ground truth, making a false-negative rate undefined until clauses are adjudicated or experimentally generated from a fixed formal \(C\). Q §Dimensions (lines 917–951) motivates this measurement problem but proves no formal-vs-prose ranking. This strengthens the matched-\(C\) design and limits claims from P’s 3/1,155 approved-move audit.
